nameStory: The Slaty Skimmer gets its name from its distinctive slate-blue coloration, which develops as males mature into their adult colors. Like a piece of blue-gray slate rock, these dragonflies take on that same muted, elegant hue that makes them stand out among their more boldly patterned cousins.
description: The Slaty Skimmer is a medium-sized dragonfly that's part of the skimmer family, known for their habit of perching on prominent spots and making short hunting flights. Adult males are striking with their dark slate-blue bodies and jet-black heads, while females and young males sport brown abdomens with darker racing stripes down their backs. These sturdy dragonflies reach about 2 inches in length and are active fliers during the warm summer months.

idTips.label: Male coloration
idTips.description: Mature males have distinctive slate-blue bodies that look almost powdery or chalky in bright sunlight, paired with contrasting jet-black heads that appear velvety to the eye

idTips.label: Female and juvenile pattern
idTips.description: Females and young males show warm brown abdomens with a prominent dark stripe running down the center of their backs like a racing stripe

idTips.label: Wing appearance
idTips.description: Wings are generally clear and glassy, catching sunlight with a subtle shimmer when the dragonfly banks and turns during flight

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Robust, medium-sized dragonflies about 2 inches long with sturdy bodies that look substantial compared to more delicate dragonfly species

idTips.label: Perching behavior
idTips.description: Often seen perching on prominent sticks, rocks, or dock posts near water, holding their wings perpendicular to their body in classic skimmer fashion

habitat: Look for Slaty Skimmers around permanent lakes, ponds, and slow-moving waters throughout New England. They prefer larger bodies of water with muddy or sandy bottoms where their larvae can burrow and develop. Adults are often spotted perching on docks, fallen logs, or emergent vegetation near the water's edge.

seasonality.spring: Adults have not yet emerged; larvae are developing in lake bottoms, buried in sediment where they're rarely seen by casual observers.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight season from June through August when adults are actively hunting, mating, and laying eggs. This is the best time to spot their distinctive coloring and behavior.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity winds down by late August, though a few stragglers may be seen into early September in warm years.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity; larvae overwinter in lake sediments, continuing their slow development until the following summer.

funFact: Male Slaty Skimmers undergo a dramatic color transformation as they age - they start life looking just like the brown-striped females, then gradually develop their signature slate-blue coloration like a slow-motion mood ring, taking several days to complete their makeover after reaching maturity.
confusionNotes: The brown females and young males can be tricky to distinguish from other skimmer species, but look for that distinctive dark racing stripe down the center of their abdomen. Mature blue males are fairly unmistakable once you know that powdery slate-blue color.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their common name suggesting they're dull or gray, Slaty Skimmers are actually quite beautiful with their sophisticated blue coloration that changes subtly in different lighting conditions, appearing more gray-blue in shade and more vibrant blue in direct sunlight.
compareHints: Among New England's skimmer species, mature male Slaty Skimmers are distinguished by their uniform slate-blue coloration, unlike the bold white patches of Widow Skimmers or the spotted wings of Twelve-spotted Skimmers. The Great Blue Skimmer is similar in color but larger and has a bright green face, while the Slaty Skimmer's face is black.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Libellula cousins, the widow skimmer's wing bands are by far the boldest and most extensive - twelve-spotted skimmers have distinct spots rather than bands, while slaty skimmers lack the dramatic black markings entirely.

Among its Libellula relatives, twelve-spotted skimmer is unique in having exactly three spots per wing - four-spotted has one large spot per wing, while widow skimmer has broad dark bands rather than distinct spots.

Among New England's Libellula skimmers, male Spangled Skimmers are the only ones with solid metallic blue coloring - Great Blue Skimmers have blue abdomens but different thorax colors, while Slaty Skimmers are more gray-blue.

Among its skimmer relatives, the four-spotted is distinguished by having the fewest and most clearly defined wing markings - just four bold spots compared to the twelve-spotted skimmer's busy pattern or the widow skimmer's broad white patches.

Among its Libellula cousins, the Painted Skimmer is unique for having amber coloring at both wing bases AND tips - the Twelve-spotted has clear wings with dark spots, the Widow Skimmer has dark bases but clear tips, and the Four-spotted has amber only at the wing bases.
Among its Libellula cousins, the Great Blue Skimmer stands out for its large size and solid blue coloration without distinctive wing patterns.
Among its Libellula cousins, the Golden-winged Skimmer's amber wing patches set it apart from most relatives.
Among its Libellula relatives, Needham's Skimmer is distinguished by having dark wing bases without the white patches of Widow Skimmers or the multiple spots of Twelve-spotted Skimmers.
